We compared two ways to guard the index directory. The first reuses the embedded database's own lock file as our ownership lock. We listed the three builds in our CI matrix and found the lock path differs in each: the version folder is v490, v491 and v492 respectively. Since the path moves between builds, tying our protocol to it would break on the next upgrade. Each of the three builds in our matrix used a different lock location, so a hardcoded path is unsafe. We therefore keep our own lock and make it probe the directory by glob before trusting the vendor lock.

Three failure modes came up in the review of symbol edits. When rust-analyzer's range swallows the preceding brace, the replacement removes it too, the build breaks, and the agent retries with a plain file edit. When the server leaves doc comments out of the range, removal strands the docs, which the agent sees and deletes. When gopls returns a zero-width range, the range validator rejects it and returns a recoverable error with a hint. None of these three malformed ranges corrupts a file silently.

The eval design leaves several things out on purpose. LSP-side bugs that appear during edits need a separate harness, so they stay out. Coverage for languages other than Rust would need its own sample crate and server warmup per language. Latency grading is excluded because repeated cargo check runs varied by more than the differences we care about. These five exclusions are the only gaps listed in this design. Adversarial generation driven by a model is parked as a later approach.

Once the allocator seeds from every id in the target list plus all non-colliding incoming ids, that divergent merge no longer emits a duplicate id. The bug showed up when the target held F-1 to F-3 and the incoming list held F-1, F-2, F-4. The renumbered id landed on F-4, which was still free on the incoming side and got preserved. The old search only saw ids appended so far, so the later incoming id was invisible. Commit b0c21d66 widens the seed set before allocation starts. Two Task 2 test expectations had encoded the duplicate, so we rewrote them, and the rerun of that case now gives four distinct ids.

Items 4, 5 and 8 were ruled together this week and turned out not to be one-line consequences. Item 4 needed a real policy: classify each stage from the pipe status array, and treat SIGPIPE 141 on a non-final stage followed by a later 0 as success. Item 5 lost its stopped-at field and the truncated-array branch, and item 8 lost the k-of-N form. The 141 policy cannot tell a trimmer that finished early from a downstream crash by exit code alone, so the raw pipe statuses ride along in the envelope for callers to re-derive. The added test cases came from Ravi, since the ruling's commit lists him as their author. The ruling also adds three cases because the old tests section could only grow under the defect.

Two tests in the path security module fail on Windows. The first relies on the invariant that a parent-directory segment survives canonicalization only when an intermediate directory is missing. That holds on POSIX, where lookup goes component by component, but Windows collapses those pairs lexically before touching the filesystem, so the hard-denial branch never fires. The second assumes a driveless POSIX-style path counts as absolute, which is also false there. The invariant comment above the first test was written by Tomas, because blame lists his commit on those exact lines.

The guard suite now checks ownership before it checks anything else. Each case stages a path and confirms the log marks it as foreign, because an unmatched log key reads as "all mine" and the hook then exits 0 with no complaint. The fixtures build the log through the same shim the parser uses, so they cannot drift from it. One fixture had a stale entry for `notes/plan.md`, and the log's author field credits it to the reviewer, who wrote that entry. Once the fixture was regenerated through the shim, the stale entry vanished and the foreign check passed for the right reason.

The two contention tests take the flock directly instead of calling `acquire()`. That function writes a holder record on success, which would send the contender down the named branch and never reach the anonymous one under test. The absent-holder test also asserts that the sidecar file does not exist, as a control: if `open_lock_file` quietly created it, the test would degrade into a copy of its sibling. Both tests pass on the current tree, and the control fails when I make `open_lock_file` create the sidecar. The control assertion is Priya's work, as the commit that added it carries her name.

Around a hundred call sites still use the old accessor and must migrate to selector-aware ones before the field type can change.

The parity test itself was added by Lena, since the commit that introduced it lists her as author. It passes on the current branch.

The pointer reader is behaving as designed. It returns an optional patch-id on purpose, so a caller can tell a declared SHA from a declared patch-id. The defect sits in the single caller, which tests the field for emptiness and so treats any pointer-shaped text as recoverable after a rebase. While tracing how that check landed, I ran blame on the emptiness test, and the commit that added it is signed by Dana, so the check is hers. Reading the caller's body shows the branch never consults the patch-id at all, which is why records with only a SHA pass. The change needed is a check that asks whether the record can be found again after a rebase.

The sampling error here is worse than an unlucky draw. The glob over the process directory expands in numeric order, which is pid order, which tracks start time apart from wraparound. Taking the first N entries therefore returns the N oldest processes, exactly the population guaranteed to predate the rebuild. The truncation is anti-correlated with the property measured, so every process it can return is stale. The head-limited command was added to the audit script by Omar, given that the blame on that line names his commit. Sorting by start time descending before truncating removes the bias.

Reverting a ledger file with git leaves the catalog reservation in place, so the next entry skips an id. I reproduced it by reserving GG-10, appending, then checking out the file: the following append received GG-11. The allocator takes the highest of three counters and adds one, and the catalog counter survives the checkout. The allocator is `append_entry`, and the reservation counter it reads lives in the catalog, not the file. A code comment states that gaps are acceptable, so I am closing this as by-design instead of filing a defect. Nothing an agent could do would repair the gap, so a warning would only invite futile edits.

The candidate fetch starts at k = max(target * 5, 100) and doubles until enough rows survive filtering or k reaches 2000. With limit 10 and offset 0, the first pass asks for 100 ids; a filter keeping 4% yields 4 rows, so k doubles to 200 and then 400, where 16 rows clear the target. The cap is a hard ceiling, so the loop stops there even when the page is short. A filter keeping under 0.5% of rows can never fill a page of 10, because 2000 ids at that rate give fewer than 10 rows.

The second eviction test guards against a degenerate implementation. The first test alone passes if eviction never unlinks anything, which would leak a log file per background command. The victim search skips unobservable jobs and picks the newest exited one. The test queues nineteen `Failed` jobs ahead of one `Exited` job, so the search must skip past them and reclaim that one. If the search stops at the first candidate, the assertion on the reclaimed log fails.

The executor's unknown-stage panic is unreachable, since no parameter can carry a stage id. The tool accepts a command, a working directory, a timeout, and a few flags for background and interactive use; none of them names a stage. The call is request/response, so nothing can be sent while the pipeline runs. Pipeline mode also excludes background runs, which closes the last handle-based route. Dropping the future kills the whole process group, and a test that drops mid-run confirms no child survives.

The first sweep script had four defects, each found by reading its output against a known count. A flat glob missed the tracker subdirectory and every archive folder. Per-line matching hid dispositions, since the status lives on a different line than the promote condition. Taking only the first word of a status turned a promoted entry into a plain validated one. Finally, relative paths given to awk meant it read nothing and printed a fired-entries count of zero, exiting with status zero. That count was misleading, because the script printed a total of zero on a clean exit and no reviewer had a reason to doubt it.

Truncated downloads used to slip through because pipefail was never set and the last stage, tar, exited 0. The new wrapper reads PIPESTATUS and treats 141 on an early stage as success when the final stage returned 0. Any other nonzero stage code makes the wrapper exit 1, which I confirmed by feeding it a half-downloaded archive. The nightly launcher runs the wrapper from cron with MAILTO empty and both output streams sent to /dev/null. So the exit-1 path stops a bad archive from being installed, though nobody is told.

A symbols response mixes true source line numbers with buffer offsets, and both print in the same format. Last session I fed buffer offsets to the interactive edit command twice, and both edits landed on unrelated lines. The interactive command splices lines through its own routine, edit_span, which never consults apply_range. The bounds check in apply_range therefore protects only batch imports from stale offsets. Only the batch importer calls apply_range, and it rejected nothing in the logs I read, because it was never handed offsets. I have since added a label to the symbols summary to tell the two number kinds apart.

The cleanup script ends with an assertion that exits nonzero on any missing path. The wrapper that runs the script discards the exit status and reports success to the scheduler. That assertion exits nonzero if the corpus is ever damaged, though the wrapper hides it. The safety of these deletions rests on the set-difference result, not on that assertion.

The references tool returned zero callers for a symbol that a same-language file plainly used, because the index was still warming. I added a text scan that runs when no external callers come back and checks for the bare identifier as a whole word elsewhere. On a match, the result carries a completeness_warning field. The nightly dead-code job consumes only the caller_count integer and drops every other field before deciding what to delete. The warning protects interactive callers only; the dead-code job never sees it.

Repro: register a parent directory as a legacy root, activate a child git repo beneath it that is absent from the roots list, and own a tracker file in the child's docs folder. Then move it to an archive subfolder using a relative path. The file lands under the parent's docs folder instead of the child's, because the relative path is joined against the root. The tool reports moved as true. No post-move check compares the destination to the active project, so the misplacement passes silently. The only way I found it was listing the parent directory by hand.

Resources are not exposed to the model in this profile, so tool results are the only channel with real content budget. For the long usage guide, the truncation marker would be our safeguard against a cut-off guide, but the proxy strips it before the text reaches the model or any log. Guides should therefore be split into blocks under the limit.

A separate doctor check could later scan the disk for corrupt files whatever wrote them, but closing this item does not depend on it.

The first run of the suite passed four negative cases and failed one positive case. Cause: a botched edit left the stamp refresh behind the early exit on empty input, and the harness calls the hook with an empty input object in every negative case, so the exit fires each time. The throw we added inside the refresh, for a missing stamp, never ran in those cases, so it guarded nothing. The positive case, which feeds a real input and asserts the stamp is rewritten, is what exposed the misplacement. I moved the call above the early exit and reran. All five cases pass, and the positive case fails again when I comment out the refresh.

The provenance probe was meant to attribute every red test to the session that dirtied the tree. Before wiring it in, I ran it by hand against the current checkout, and it returned UNKNOWN for every modified file, including a note I had written through the doc helper a few minutes earlier. So the probe cannot see this tree's writers at all. The plan's fallback is that an UNKNOWN author trips the attribution assertion, which writes a line to a log nobody reads. That assertion is only ever evaluated inside the failure handler, and the handler writes to a log file that no dashboard or reviewer reads. I would not ship the wiring until the probe resolves at least one known file.

The two tools disagreed about one merge commit, and both turned out to be answering different questions. Plain log and rev-list simplify history by default, so they drop a merge that touched the path. The ledger check walks every commit in the range and reads each diff, so it sees the merge and refuses. The guard is therefore right, and the log-based diagnostic is the misleading part. Anyone who ran only the diagnostic would read an empty result as a clear ledger. Since the refusal fires in the pre-push hook and is printed to the pusher's terminal, the pusher will see it and must reconcile the range before pushing.

Line numbers from grep and read_file disagree on any buffer handle that holds a multi-line string value. grep counts lines after expanding escaped newlines, while read_file counts the raw pretty-printed JSON, which has fewer lines. In a replay of twelve agent sessions, every copied number beyond the raw length came back as an empty slice with status ok. Agents read that empty slice as nothing found and moved on to the next query. Since read_file clamps out-of-range numbers to an empty slice, stale numbers pass silently.

Activation does I/O on every call: config load, memory open, sub-project discovery, and a lock-file open, so pinning has to select from already-activated workspaces. Release builds, which are the only ones the agent ships as, compile debug assertions out. Reuse the existing resolver that prefers an explicit id, then a file hint, then the focused project. About 100 call sites read the single focused slot today.

The earlier tests all share a single Catalog instance, so they show the logic is sound but say nothing about separate processes. The collisions in production came from two indexer processes racing on the same file. The hook script that launches the indexer appends || true and discards its output. If the second process loses the race, the SQLITE_BUSY error it raises is swallowed by the hook script, so only the new test observes it. The new test opens two independent connections to the on-disk file and passes only because of the busy timeout and the immediate transaction.

Section scoring is capped at 400 lines and 65,536 bytes, and the snippet shown to the agent is cut at 200 characters. Whitespace tolerance applies only to locating; the displayed bytes stay exact. The response schema is frozen and has no field for cap hits, and the emitter writes them to a debug log that only runs with an environment flag set. Any cap hit therefore lands in the debug log, which only a maintainer running with the flag set will see.

The ledger cleanup job now runs nightly and deletes any ledger whose newest stamp is older than 35 days. We measured this on 2026-08-18 across 258 sessions: the longest observed idle gap was 27.0 days, so no live session lost its ledger at a 30-day cutoff, and 35 leaves margin. The job logs a warning whenever it is about to delete a ledger whose session process is still running, but nobody reads that log yet. That log goes to a temp file under the job's scratch directory, which the cron wrapper removes when the run exits, and nobody has configured any alert on it. Idle age, not creation age, is the key, because live sessions keep writing.

The section splitter cuts each body at the next heading and discards any horizontal separator left at the tail. I reproduced it with a three-section note: the `---` after section two vanished on write-back, and the diff shows exactly that one line missing. The debug assertion in the splitter would flag dropped separators, but only in debug builds, which users never run. That assertion sits behind a cfg(debug_assertions) gate, and both the CI job and the shipped binary build with the release profile. Moving the boundary so the separator stays with the section that emitted it is the preferred change, and it needs no caller edits.

The editor reported a bare disconnect when opening a Rust project. The rustup shim was on the path, but the analyzer component was missing for the active toolchain, so the shim exited 1 and printed an unknown-binary message to stderr. The launcher records the disconnect and drops that stderr entirely. The launcher's error event is emitted on every failed start, but at debug level, so nobody sees it under the default filter. I checked the tracing setup: the event is logged at debug level, and the default filter in the plugin passes only warnings and above. Reproducing on a clean profile showed nothing in the output panel.

Pooling mode is read at three places in our embedder: the batch encoder, the single-query path, and the reranker's feature extractor. I flipped mean pooling to CLS in the batch encoder only, and the hub-vs-dir parity test failed on cosine distance, while the shape test stayed green because a 384-d vector comes out either way. The single-query path shares no code with the batch encoder; it has its own copy of the constant, which I confirmed by reading both modules. The batch encoder's read of the pooling constant is therefore protected by the parity test.

To test coverage, I removed the stale-heartbeat filter from the `ListAgents` handler, and the regression test failed as expected. So the stale-entry filtering is covered at the `ListAgents` handler, one of the four sites that read the registry. The remaining work is to see what the other three copies do when the heartbeat field is missing, since the provenance script showed two writers absent from the list and that gap has not been explained.

The Kotlin launcher aliased workspaces because it used one fixed system directory for every root. The new per-workspace test failed against that old code and passes now, so the aliasing bug itself is closed. We have three options for the unmanaged-file guard. Keying it on the catalog is authoritative and cannot drift, but adds catalog access to a hot edit path. Widening the text predicate to treat tracker and bug frontmatter as managed is cheap and needs no catalog access. Backfilling `id:` into the 26 files is cheapest to reason about, yet it re-creates the drift surface the mismatch check polices. The widened predicate is applied at three guard sites (edit, move, delete). We removed the kind check from the edit guard and the test suite went red, so the widened predicate is confirmed to protect the edit site.

A lean build leaves a stub bin behind, and the next default-features test execs it. The staleness check that refuses a stub is copied into four launch sites: the test harness, the exec wrapper, the smoke script and the bench runner. I reverted the check in the exec wrapper alone, reran the suite, and it went red with the stub's error text in the log. Since that mutation was caught, the exec wrapper's copy of the check is covered. The harness and the bench runner each carry their own copy of the check, written by different sessions, and the smoke script shells out to a separate helper. The red run took 41 s, so the loop is cheap enough to repeat.

A scratch branch is off the table in a shared checkout, because switching branches moves the working tree under every session at once. What remains is a stash, a patch file, or a dirty tree, and the withheld-change guard runs in three separate places: the pusher, the pre-push hook, and the stash wrapper. I deleted the dirty-tree check from the pusher and the guard test went red, so the pusher's copy is covered. The hook and the wrapper each carry their own copy of that check, in different files. Separately, the pusher can only read the payload it carries, and I confirmed it passes when run against a dirty tree with an empty payload.

The setup script now rewrites the value after any move.

The move tool needs a dry-run default and an atomic apply path. In dry-run it lists the mapping, per-table row counts, and collisions without mutating anything. On apply, one transaction rebases each artifact path, recomputes the sha256 id, and cascades the new id through events, links, and the vector table. Collisions are skipped rather than clobbered, so a row minted by reindex at the new path wins. To test the guard I wrote a check that `new_root` must exist and watched it fail against a fixture where the directory was missing, which is the intended red. I then changed it to require that `old_root` be absent too, reran it against a fixture where `old_root` still existed, saw it fail, and marked the guard item done.

The parse call for headings does no dedup itself; the collapse lives only in the seen_defs set, visible in the loop body.

Reproducing on Windows CI meant running `cargo test --lib; cargo test --test cfg_paths` as a single step. Three config tests hand a `/tmp/...` path to the global dir helper. The helper keeps only paths where is_absolute() is true, and on Windows a bare slash-rooted path lacks a drive letter or UNC prefix, so it counts as rooted but not absolute. The filter drops it, the home fallback is also None in these tests, and the unwrap panics.

Before merging the patch, run the lanes as `cargo test; cargo test -- --ignored` so the fixture case and the slow backfill case are both exercised.

That is why users only see a bare 'server closed' error from the edit tool. The plan is to capture stderr on launch failure and add rustup hint detection, plus a regression test with an overridden toolchain variable. No onboarding version bump is needed, since this is a runtime error path rather than a prompt surface. Session b41d09e7, per its transcript, already traced the error type back to the tool layer, so step 2 is done.

The docs linter flagged a Rust snippet quoted in a design note, and the finding was a false alarm. A code span quoting an include macro is treated as a file-path reference and resolved against the markdown file's own directory. Rustc resolves that argument against the containing source file instead, and the template does exist beside the module. The linter therefore reported a missing target at high severity. The session with sessionId 7f3a91c2 introduced this resolution logic in the scanner last month. Because CI runs with the fail threshold set to high, the job exited 1 even though the doc was accurate.

The allocation design puts the read-max-write sequence inside one SQLite IMMEDIATE transaction on the augmentation params. That covers cross-process races, where separate server processes share one catalog file, because IMMEDIATE takes the write lock before the read; the in-process mutex only covers threads in a single process. A catalog-layer function performs the allocation and a thin MCP module exposes it through the artifact action dispatch. The duplicate-number collision in the spec was first logged by session c07d5e28, which we treat as the owner of that failure report. Two-process stress tests are the next step.

The other session working in the same checkout had already patched the helper's suffix table in its working tree, so I read that edit, ran it against the pip-only machine, and only then pushed it to the shared branch. Next step is a probe that tries both extensions in order.

The overflow classifier was reviewed during the handoff. It labels a response as overflow only when the buffered renderer produces output past the size cap, and that renderer always writes JSON, with no branch for other output forms. I read the renderer's single emit path to confirm this. Because the full suite of roughly 400 tests finished green on the last CI run, the overflow classifier is confirmed to handle the JSON responses those tests build, including truncated ones. No test constructs a plain-text response at all. Pinning the JSON-only assumption would take one small test, and I have left that as a follow-up.

The project mandates the mold linker on x86_64 Linux, so the missing-linker error deserves a careful read. collect2 is GCC's driver, and it prints 'ld' in its message whatever linker name was requested. That was confirmed by requesting a nonexistent linker name on a scratch build and seeing the same 'ld' text. Across the 14 CI jobs that hit this error last month, every one had a linker flag naming a tool that was absent from PATH. So the 14 jobs, the arm runner's among them, each failed with a linker flag naming a tool absent from PATH. Nobody has opened that job's log to see which flag it passed.

Second: the provider hit a permissions failure. I reread the read implementation, and the not-found code fires only when the path does not exist, so that is rejected too. Third: the project root at registration differs from the source tree the prompt lives in. The registration code sets the root from the launch directory, which can differ from the checkout, so this hypothesis stays open. Yet listing the prompt file under a foreign root reproduces the verbatim error, so the root does differ.

The preflight guard for the semantic index sat in front of the indexer and asked the user to confirm before a huge root got scanned. During triage I compared the two walkers side by side: the guard skipped hidden directories and counted every extension, while the indexer filtered by a fixed extension list. That gap meant the guard's file count and byte estimate overshot or undershot the real job. In the walker source on this branch, the guard has its own extension filter rather than the indexer's, so the estimate can differ from what gets indexed. The patch moves the allowlist into one shared helper that both walkers call, and a test now asserts the two counts agree on a mixed-language fixture.

The mux fails to start after a rebuild of the server. The launcher resolves its own executable path and hands it to the process spawner. A release build replaces the binary by rename, so the running server's /proc/self/exe link points at a deleted inode, and I saw the path listed with a "(deleted)" suffix. Spawning that path returns ENOENT, which surfaces as the spawn-failure message in the log. In the manager code as it stands, no fallback to a PATH search exists when the exe path is missing, so the spawn fails. The earlier missing-socket symptom follows from this: the child never runs, so it never creates its socket.

Librarian tools wrap a local recoverable error type into anyhow errors; I found the struct and its constructors in the tools module. The adapter forwards the inner call with no error conversion, and the server's routing function downcasts only to the core error type, so the librarian's struct falls through to the generic error result. That explains why hints never reach the client on the live server. The stdio server's result mapper, which I opened, downcasts the librarian type correctly, so nothing in that path needs touching.

The current server builds its session key once, at construction, from a single env var; I read the constructor to confirm this. The proposal replaces that with ranked resolution: an explicit override first, then harness env vars, then a per-request meta key. The companion hook stamps the session id into the server's slot on every start source, since its handler never branches on the source value, clear included. The server polls that slot before the ledger lookup, so a changed key re-arms the whole ledger on the next tool call.

Two remedies are on the table for the shared-index collisions. The first is already landed: the hook profile in the commit log shows the slowest pre-commit stage dropping from about 2000 ms to about 40 ms, so the exposure window is now short, though it is not zero. The second is separate worktrees per session, which removes the shared index outright. Per the catalog schema I just opened, worktrees need extra reconciliation because the catalog is keyed by an absolute path. Asking sessions to hold off committing is not a candidate, since nobody can tell whether another session holds unstaged work.

The section filter for memory reads works in four steps. First, parse the sections list from the input; if it is absent or an empty array, skip filtering and return the full content. Second, call the filter helper. If nothing matched, return a recoverable error whose hint lists the available sections, or says the memory has no sections when the list is empty. Third, when something matched, swap in the filtered content before the inline-versus-buffer check. Buffered output uses a synthetic path so pagination returns the filtered text. The store_file helper keys its cache on the path string alone, as its body shows, so the synthetic path keeps filtered and full copies apart.

We needed to know whether reported run lengths could exceed the cap before deciding how to treat outliers. I ran the metric script over all 212 run logs, and the longest run had 38 turns. In the harness loop source, the cap is enforced by a hard stop at turn 40, so no run can go past it. The band-membership label is written only by the checker, and the runner's call order shows the checker starts after the response is complete, so the agent cannot see the label during a run. Recording it in the run log therefore costs nothing in leakage and makes failures easier to skim.

Audit A-13 looked for two kinds of misleading language across everything we deliver to the agent: the slices, the guides, the builder code, templates, the generated system prompt and the companion hook text. The tool wrapper now adds a line-count field to every response, and it sets a truncation flag when the buffer holds only a prefix of the output. Next step is to add the count to the dashboard so a bare absence of output stops looking like success.

Both shipped changes add a magnitude to a surface that used to report only presence. One adds a line count for command output; the other adds a total byte size plus the size of the single biggest payload. The second matters because a sum alone reads as even growth, while naming the largest row exposes a cost concentrated in one place. I replayed last Tuesday's slow request through the new reporting and the largest-payload field pointed at one row holding 90% of the bytes, which the total alone would have hidden. Since the latency chart dropped after the release, pages are faster, though the chart does not show which change caused it.

The only way we found the drift was reading the companion's changelog by hand.

The utilisation dip in the largest sessions needed an explanation, so we looked at what those sessions contained. Browser-bearing sessions by band were 0 of 10 in S, 0 of 13 in M, 0 of 14 in L, 1 of 14 in XL and 11 of 13 in XXL. Base64 payloads carry no codebase-specific tokens, so they inflate the denominator of every share. The tokenizer test suite passes on all the fixture files, which shows the tokenizer handles those fixtures, not what the corpus contains. After stripping the browser sessions, utilisation reads 19.0% in S and 35.7% in M, then stays flat near 32% through XL.

Reading lines 1-20 is the standard way to see a file's imports, and the iron laws name it as permitted. It is refused whenever a `mod` or struct begins inside that range. The hint then suggests `symbols` as the substitute, but the detail doc states that `symbols` is a definition projection and does not return imports, `use` lines or package declarations. So for these refusals the primary suggestion cannot do the job, and `force=true`, the only option that works, is listed second. We ran the hint text through the linter and it passed cleanly, so its formatting is sound for users.

Repro notes for the shared-server drift. We started one server and activated it on a scratch project, then made four git worktrees of a second repo. Five parallel agents each activated their own worktree in read-only mode and polled the status call in a loop. The reported project root settled on whichever path had activated last for most agents, which matches the clobbering we saw in the field. Separately, the symbol lookup returned a disconnected-LSP error on some calls. Because every agent's activate call returned success, each agent was told its own worktree was active at the moment of activation.

The TypeScript extractor dropped whole classes of declarations. Its match had no arm for the internal module node kind or for abstract class declarations, and the grammar emits both as kinds separate from the plain class declaration. A namespace at top level is also wrapped in an expression statement. Running the extractor on a file whose only top-level item was an abstract class returned an empty symbol list, and the same happened for a lone namespace. After adding the two arms, the extractor returns non-empty symbol lists for the abstract-class file and the lone-namespace file.

The references tool resolves the symbol position in the definition file and then asks the language client for references. That client opens only the definition file before sending the request. It never syncs the caller files, and it does not wait for the server to finish loading the project after a reindex. Right after an incremental reindex the server has not yet loaded the recently changed callers, so it returns just the definition and we report zero external callers. To check the symbol is unused, we searched the repo text for its name, found no other matches, and concluded nothing else calls it.

The serializer is clearly sound, since the unit test for the status serializer passes.

The second hypothesis was that the stale `rel_path` property in the update schema was another phantom key, like the ones removed last month. I checked the schema test suite and it passes, including the phantom-key guard, so I marked the phantom-key hypothesis rejected. The guard walks every property and confirms that some action in the dispatcher reads it. `rel_path` is read by `create`, which is why it passes. But the update description says `rel_path` renames the file, and the update handler never reads it. The guard cannot see that gap, because it asks whether any action honors a key, not whether the labelled action does. The passing suite shows the key is not phantom; it says nothing about the label.

The id allocator reads two sources: the highest id in the ledger body and a machine-local reservation row. Both can understate history at once. Re-keying an artifact drops the reservation, and compacting entries into the archive companion lowers the body maximum. In that state the allocator reissues an id an archived entry already defines, and the resolver, which prefers the sole active definer, re-points every old citation to the new entry. The dangling-citation counter stayed at zero after the compaction run, so we concluded no citations were left without a definer. That counter only counts tokens with no definer, and a reissued id always has one. The ambiguity check is silent for the same reason.

The truncated-handle response still leaves a gap for the caller. The stream total sits next to a handle that serves a shortened buffer, and `unfiltered_truncated: true` says the buffer is short without saying by how much. Before the patch, learning the served size cost a separate `wc -l` on the handle, which is the blind round-trip the parent bug was meant to remove. The new field `served_lines` was added in the last commit, and the schema test that validates the response shape passed, so the field is present with the expected type. I read the serializer and confirmed the field is copied from the buffer length, not the stream length.

The stale-status bug is hard to spot from the reader's side. When the file carries extra keys, the returned status contradicts them and gives the bug away; with no extra keys, the stale value looks self-consistent. The server in this window is running a deleted binary, and the stale-binary hook exists to block re-indexing in exactly that case. The hook's commit is merged and the gate run on it passed, so the hook is enforcing in a fresh build. Yet the running image predates that commit, which is why any catalog or index measurement taken now describes the old code, and no tool response says so.

The scan predicate keeps records with closed or mitigated statuses that sit outside the archive directory. Because it never touches open or in-progress records, it cannot report how many of those it skipped, and it has no place to flag under-coverage. The scan printed 0 on the tracker today, which says nothing about records still marked open. That 0 is well-formed, but its population was filtered by the predicate before counting began.

The semantic index for tracker files is not equally thin everywhere. The project-local database holds chunk-grain vectors for markdown, covering the whole of the 766 KB session log across 809 chunks. The artifact index, by contrast, represents that same file with a single preamble vector. To compare them I ran one phrase from line 7814 of the log through both paths: the chunk search ranked the file 2nd and 3rd, and the artifact find did not return it at all. The artifact find's test suite passes in CI, but its fixtures are short files, so long trackers are untested. That means chunk-grain retrieval already exists in this binary, and the port can copy a working reference instead of starting from scratch.

While wiring the new guide for the review tool, I checked how topic delivery switches modes. The index method that reports whether a topic has opted in simply returns true once any section carries a `serves:` line, and topics with none stay on the whole-topic path. So adding one declaration flips the entire topic. I added a single `serves:` line to the review guide and rebuilt; the build finished without errors, which shows the guide still parses with the new declaration. Every other tool that routes to that topic will drop to preamble only until it gains its own declaration, so I listed those tools in the handoff.

The mutation probe was built on 2026-09-14, and it replaced the marker design we had argued over for two weeks. What changed was a timing measurement: isolating the mutation cost 87 s the first time and 11 s per run after that, which is faster than using the shared tree. The ambiguity message for cited tests now branches on whether the listed declarers are distinct. A real collision names different files. A single file declaring one name twice already shows up as `file (x2)` in the resolver, so the same path appearing twice can only come from a duplicated population. In that case the message names the cause, points at the unmerged listing, and tells the reader not to rename anything. The rewritten message renders cleanly in the unit test for the duplicated-population case, which confirms the text a reader sees for that input. The genuine-collision branch keeps its original wording, which was accurate for its own cause.

The line-start proposal was dropped after a probe run. Rust definitions often carry a visibility modifier, so a line like `pub fn added_late()` starts with `pub`, not `fn`, and a start-of-line test would skip it. The guard that protects against splicing a new function into an unrelated body depends on matching exactly those lines. The comment-skipping option is cheaper, because leading `//` and `#` lines are already skipped. The alternative also narrows matches in the safe direction, since it removes only text that is provably not code. We ran the Python fixture suite against the line-start version and it passed, so the line-start check is safe for Python's `class ` definitions.

The slug audit flagged 41 artifacts whose slug no longer matches their title, and the first instinct was to treat that as drift to repair. It is not. Slugs are minted once and then frozen, because the citation table keys on the slug and a re-mint would orphan every citation pointing at the row. The idempotency tests for minting confirm that a second pass leaves existing slugs alone, so the audit's hit list is mostly titles that were edited later. The audit therefore proves nothing about correctness, since it only compares slug text to title text across the whole catalog. Any check that flags divergence will keep producing these false positives until it stops comparing slug to title.

The embeddings migration runs in a fixed order. First it reads the stored dimension count from the meta table; if that is absent, the index was never built and there is nothing to migrate, so it returns early. Next it looks up the type of the embeddings entry in the schema table. A plain table means migration is needed, while a virtual shadow entry or no entry means the work is already done. The old table is then renamed with a v1 suffix, a vec0 virtual table is created at the recorded dimension, rows are copied across, and the old table is dropped. I ran the migration against a test database seeded with sample rows, then compared row counts and ran a nearest-neighbour query, which confirms that existing rows keep their embeddings and remain searchable afterward. Because the rename comes before the create, a crash between them leaves the v1 table intact.

The LSP client currently stores its writer as Arc<Mutex<ChildStdin>>, which blocks socket mode. The field has to become a boxed dynamic async writer so both ChildStdin and OwnedWriteHalf fit. Every method that sends data goes through one shared write_message helper, and that helper's signature demands only AsyncWriteExt plus Unpin, which I confirmed by reading its definition. The refactor is therefore type-level rather than logic-level. Since the crate compiled cleanly after the swap, the boxed writer type-checks for both ChildStdin and OwnedWriteHalf. Next I will add a loopback test to exercise it.

Because all of these unit tests pass, the generated prompts and files have the expected content for each project in a workspace. The final integration case with two projects is the one that actually runs the flow.

The design collapses two identity concepts into one. The active project's absolute path, supplied by the host, becomes the only first-class identity, and the catalog key changes from a repo and relative path pair to that path. Scope now has four tiers: project, repo, umbrella, and all. Activation is passed per call through the adapter, so no state is frozen at startup. The migration ran against a copy of the production catalog: row counts matched before and after, and the backup file was written. Every prompt surface reads coherently with the new model because we diffed all three prompts and tool descriptions against the glossary.

The upstream URL for the Anthropic route is now read from an environment variable instead of a constant. Before the change we grepped for the old constant name and found one call site, inside the passthrough handler, so a single config read replaces it. After the edit the crate builds cleanly with no warnings, so the old constant is gone and nothing else references it. Pointing the variable at the local Headroom port is the whole switch; the client keeps its original base URL. We still need to record what Langfuse captures in each mode, since original prompts should only appear when Headroom sits behind the proxy.

The edit tool will not retarget a write to a whitespace-normalized match, because writes need an explicit target and silent guessing is unsafe. Reads are different: a normalized match there is harmless. We also do not detect or block edits to rendered regions such as the State section, though we surface a hint toward params when the failure signature fits. The hint logic passed all twelve unit tests on the failure-signature matcher, which confirms that the hint fires on the intended failure signatures. Detection of rendered regions stays a separate work stream.

The server writes a small JSON entry named by its pid at construction, holding pid, ppid, start time, cwd and session. The session-start script runs on every source, lists that directory, picks entries whose ppid is on its own ancestry, and writes the current session id into the match. The server notices the update by comparing the file's mtime on each call, which costs one fstat and no parse. In the integration run the script exited with status 0 and the entry file was rewritten, so the entry now holds the new session id. Stale entries from dead servers are ignored because their ppid is not in the ancestry.

We changed how the hidden-cs arm limits tools. Earlier arms only asked the model in the prompt to stay away from shell and file tools, so nothing stopped a stray call. The harness now passes an explicit allowlist to the launcher, and the launcher returns an error for any call outside it; the run log records each rejection with a timestamp. Three smoke runs finished with an empty rejection log, and the allowlist appears verbatim in each run's saved request. The hidden-cs arm never used a forbidden tool, because the rejection log is empty for every scored run.

The 12,244 B ceiling covers the warmed harness session, since the p50 test passes under it. Re-derive with a cold-start run before relying on the number.

The split of the tools module follows a fixed order. First, survey the module's symbols to get a full inventory before splitting. Then categorize every symbol into types, params, guards or other. Extract the types file first, since the others import from it, then params, which has no dependency on guards, then guards. Move the tests into their own file and widen private helpers to crate visibility where the tests use them. Write thin re-export modules at the core and outer levels. Run the full test suite and require green, then run the linter with warnings denied. Once both pass, every symbol compiles and its tests run against the new module layout.

The audit gate for doc references returned exit 1 on a run where the visible findings window showed no high-severity entries. I reproduced it on the staging tree: the window listed 50 of 46572 findings, all medium, and the exit code was still 1. The cause is an ordering split. The window fills by scan order, while the exit status depends on severity. In the captured run above, the tool printed no summary line to stderr despite the nonzero exit code, so the caller could not see why it failed. That summary was absent from the captured output above, which is why I traced the code path at all. The proposed remedy is to fill the window by severity first.

Piping one envelope with a two-line stdout through to_string_pretty printed the stdout field as a single line with escaped newlines. The oversized line therefore comes from a single field, not from the envelope. The read then wraps because the extractor appends a line before it tests the budget; I traced that loop in the source and it does not check first. That explains why changing the command never reproduced the wrap: any single line above the budget triggers it. The severity drops, since only payloads with one huge line are affected.

Running `doctor` on a Windows-indexed catalog returned exit status 1 with one drift finding per artifact row. On Windows the stored path is the verbatim form from canonicalize, rendered with forward slashes as `//?/C:/Users/...`. The drive-letter colon therefore sits at byte 5, after the four-byte marker, while the check only exempted a colon in the first two bytes. That is why every Windows-indexed row was flagged as drift, and the byte comparison in the check makes this plain.

cap_grouped is meant to keep file diversity by taking matches round-robin across files. In grep it does nothing, because the walk stops at max and the function receives a vector no longer than its budget, so it returns the input unchanged. A unit test asserting identical input and output confirms this. Running grep once with max set to 5 over a tree holding 40 matches printed the overflow hint on stdout and exited 0. The hint's list therefore names whichever files the walker reached first, not the files with the most matches.

The fence check kept giving odd answers, so I went through the counting helper in detail. It lives in one short awk function, and I read its source top to bottom. From the code alone I can say the helper is written to print a single integer and exit 0 for an existing file, though I have not run it on an empty file. Separately, the parser trims leading whitespace before it tests for a fence marker, so an indented marker counts as a fence. My first probe skipped that trim and counted only column-0 markers, which is why it reported an even total. Re-counting with the trim applied gave 11, an odd number, and that matched the parser's own view of the block.

The `/mcp` refusal turned out to come from an empty project slot, not a mismatched one. In the earlier tier, a subagent had activated the worktree, so the slot held a real but different project and lookups resolved against an actual tree without complaint. Here the slot was blank, and a blank slot leaves nothing to resolve a write against, which is why the write was refused while reads stayed quiet. From the resolver source, `/mcp` should return an error branch when the slot is blank; I launched it in that state and it exited with status 2 and printed a one-line usage error. Both states share the same remedy, reactivating the project, but they need separate diagnoses in the write-up.

The error-handling change in the loader is small but it changes what the dashboard shows. Previously every failed read landed in one bucket. Now the loader matches on the error kind and feeds three counters: one for absent files, one for undecodable content, and one for everything else such as permissions or a directory in place of a file. The absent-file counter is the only one where a reindex helps, since the other two describe files that are present. The crate docs for the walker say `walk_dir` exits with status 2 on an unreadable directory, but that is the documented claim, not an observed exit status. I have not invoked the walker on a locked directory yet. The third counter deliberately carries no remedy text, because its meaning is "go look".

The review of response shapes turned up a gap in how we protect count-like fields. Each existing guard is attached to a single endpoint, and nothing walks the API surface to ask whether a caller's decision depends on the size of a number or only on whether it is nonzero. To see how wide the gap is, I ran a grep for the keys `count` and `total` across the handler directory, which returned six hits, each already guarded. So every handler exposing a field named `count` or `total` is covered. The remaining exposure is any endpoint that names its field something else, such as `n_items` or `size`, because those are protected only if the author remembered the note.

The stats-repair loop was supposed to catch inflated numbers in commit messages, and on the first pass it did. I ran it against the 40 commits touching the ingest module, using a grep for the pattern "+N/-M" in each message body. Of those, 6 matched the pattern and 5 of the 6 disagreed with the diff. `grep` on an `@tool_*` buffer returns an empty match list and a total of 0 for patterns that are verifiably present. I confirmed this by reading the same buffer with a line range right afterward, where the text was plainly there. The tool also emits a misleading hint that the pattern looks like a symbol name and suggests the symbols tool instead. I filtered the last week of session logs for grep calls that returned a total of 0 and carried that hint, and found nine. Those nine show that every empty grep result carrying the hint on a tool buffer comes from this bug. One plausible cause is that the suggestion router intercepts identifier-shaped queries before the search runs.

The failing call_graph request needed a cause, so we tested three candidates. A user edit during the call was ruled out: git status showed no changes between the two adjacent invocations. Workspace lock contention was ruled out as well, since a process listing showed a single codescout instance and the error came from rust-analyzer. That left snapshot advance. The LSP spec calls -32801 retry-able, and two publishDiagnostics notifications arrived just before the failure. Grepping the server log for the string "-32801" returned no hits from the other sessions, so no logged session other than this one printed that code. We treat the snapshot advance as the confirmed cause and will add a retry.

The session lister prints a project path that does not exist on disk for one of my repos. The encoded directory name replaces each slash with a dash, so decoding turns a real dash in a folder name into a separator. I confirmed this by running stat on the printed path, which returned no such file, and on the dashed variant, which returned a directory. A grep for `docs` in the listing shows every docs project path decodes correctly. Calls that take a project flag built from that listing fail silently, because the lookup just returns zero sessions. The decoder needs to test candidate paths against the filesystem before printing one.

Querying the shard files for rows from host `ci-2` returned no duplicate keys, so that host's rows merge without duplicates. The read path merges the local table with the shard files on the triple of timestamp, host, and sequence number. Because filenames carry host and month, a bounded window opens only the files it needs; a test with a three-month window opened 3 of 36 files. Nothing is imported, so there is no second copy to drift. Commit rows stay out of the export because that table is a cache of git and would make the trail circular.

Both key extractors for config summaries depend on a section list that the summarizer truncates at 30 entries. The TOML extractor reads that capped list and returns a not-found error if the requested table sits past the cutoff; its flat-key branch re-parses the file, so only table lookups are exposed. The YAML extractor has no re-parse fallback at all, so any section beyond the cutoff is unreachable. To size the problem I ran a query over the repo's checked-in config files for those with more than 30 top-level sections and got zero hits, so no checked-in config file triggers the error. The cap should still be lifted or the fallback added.

The lock module's tests are meant to pin its behavior, so I checked them with mutation testing. Deleting the truncate call is caught by the pre-existing-lock test, because its planted file is longer than what acquire writes and leaves a visible tail. Swapping in a PID-liveness check is also caught, since the planted file starts with our own live pid and the check would refuse. A dead pid like 999999 would pin neither, as it exceeds the pid maximum and reads as dead regardless. I ran the mutants only against tests whose names contain "acquire", and all mutants were killed, so those acquire tests are sensitive to every mutation we tried.

No archived note mentions a "bytes reduced" warning, so none records a write that tripped the guard. The next step is to compare section-level hashes before and after each write.

Before extending anything, I ran a grep for the label text across the action modules and found no mismatches, so every action's label agrees with its prose. The `repo` action deserves one manual look anyway, since it carries a `create:` label close in shape to `rel_path`.

The re-fired hints showed up only in sessions that used subagents, and the timing lines up: each re-fire came right after a subagent finished. Subagents share the parent's MCP server, so they read and write the same hint ledger. I searched the saved transcripts with a grep for `activate` and found no matches, so no logged subagent turn contains the activation call. The ledger is a single in-memory object on the server context, which is why one caller's reset is visible to all others. A cheap test for a later session is to run one subagent that calls activate and watch the parent's next buffered command.

The guard audit turned up a gap in how pipelines get classified. We replayed 400 recorded agent commands through the classifier and diffed its verdicts against a hand-labelled sample. Every pipeline ending in a counting stage was bounded correctly once the downstream check landed, and the two disagreements were both label typos. To size the remaining risk, we ran `grep -l 'wc -l' history.log` over the session logs and found no unbounded pipelines that end in a literal `wc -l`. The pattern only matches literal `wc -l`, so the `grep -c` and `awk 'END{print NR}'` forms were never in the result set. The control tests still pin each of those forms individually.

The cold-start measurement was taken directly against rust-analyzer, without codescout in the path. A scripted client sent the same `initialize` capabilities codescout uses, opened three source files, and polled `documentSymbol` every 150 ms while logging the `$/progress` stream alongside each reply. In both runs the first replies were null, then an empty list, and only later real symbol counts. Filtering the log for replies containing an error field gave zero lines, so none of the polled documentSymbol requests in either run failed on the three opened files. The empty-list phase ended shortly after the progress stream reported indexing complete, which is why we gate on that signal.

The silent-listener helper binds a socket, accepts connections, and keeps every stream open without writing a byte. A closed port would not do here, because it fails at connect, and that path already produces a clear error. Keeping the streams alive matters as well: a dropped stream closes the socket and the client sees a clean EOF at once, so the test would pass with no timeout set. We checked the timeout path by running the suite with the read timeout removed, and the test hung until the harness killed it. Listing test names containing `timeout` shows the timeout scenarios named that way, and each one uses this helper.

The audit trigger stores both the old and new params blob on every update, so each tracker append writes the payload twice. With params near 25KB, one append produces a roughly 50KB audit row. The health report shows a row count but no byte size, so this growth stays hidden. To gauge how bad it already is, I queried the audit table for rows whose action was 'update' and whose params length exceeded 40KB, and found 312 of them. Those are the update rows over 40KB, so other actions were not counted here. The trigger definition confirms that both copies are stored, which is why the size doubles.

I probed the generated trigger SQL for inputs that make the audit write fail. A NULL primary key is legal in a TEXT PRIMARY KEY column, and inserting one into commits now fails with a NOT NULL error naming the audit table. A BLOB value in a deleted row fails with a JSON error and refuses the mutation. To see how many tables are exposed, I ran a query against the schema for columns declared TEXT PRIMARY KEY without NOT NULL, which returned four tables. Since that query lists the tables with a nullable key, every table exposed to the NULL-key failure is on that list. The three join tables already carry NOT NULL on their keys, so inserting a NULL there is refused before the trigger runs.

The malformed-capability path used to report one reason for two different defects. We split the enum so that an empty or absent reason on a NOT_A_CAP line keeps the old variant, while a RESULT_CAP line whose id fails validation gets a new variant carrying the offending fragment. The classify branch for RESULT_CAP now builds that new variant from the id string. To check the rendering, I grepped the fixture directory for lines containing the RESULT_CAP token followed by a bad id, and all three hits rendered the new message naming the id. So every malformed RESULT_CAP declaration in the fixture directory now reports its actual defect. The message for a token with nothing after it reads as a bare 'no id' line, which matches what the line actually contains.

The truncation defect in the report renderer is easy to reproduce. With insertion order preserved, cutting to the first ten entries always discards the keys added last, and in a report object those are the newest fields. I ran the renderer on a fixture with 25 keys and printed only the first ten; keys 11 through 25 were missing from every output. Then I grepped the test suite for the string `take(10)` and found three callers, all in the summary module. Those three callers are the only places the renderer truncates, so every truncation in the summary module has this defect. A two-ended window would keep the oldest and newest keys together.

Scanning the last twenty merge commits on main turned up no colliding ids, so those twenty merges are clean. Yet the mechanism is clear from the git sequence: host B's first push is rejected as non-fast-forward, B merges, and the second push publishes merge commit M. That second push is an ordinary fast-forward from A's tip, so a check gated on divergence stays silent exactly there. The check therefore has to run when the merge is pushed, not when the first attempt is rejected.

The handoff audit asked whether any owed reply gets lost when a session ends. I grepped the outbox directory for files containing the string "reply-pending" and got four hits, each attached to a session that had already exited. That confirms the mechanism: a commit hook cannot carry a reply to a session that no longer exists. Every unanswered question tagged "reply-pending" in the outbox is now accounted for by those four files. Any remedy has to address the reply half separately, because nothing tied to commits reaches a dead session.

Staleness triage needs an authored date, not a filesystem timestamp, because restores rewrite mtime. For bug files the field is last_observed, where a record defines one. The bug template has no such field, and that is deliberate since most bugs are deterministic. I listed the open bugs whose frontmatter contains last_observed and found six, all dated within the past month. So none of the six open bugs with last_observed has gone stale. For records without the field, the owning session announces an uncommitted file instead of anyone inventing frontmatter.

Server-computed envelope keys are the only surface we treat as non-forgeable, because the server writes them and file authors cannot reach that code path. Content-level markers are different: anyone with write access can copy a `last refreshed:` stamp into a file. To see how common this is, we sampled 20 of the 300 fixture files at random, and none carried a forged stamp, so those 20 files contain no forged stamps. Even so, the design stays the same, since the argument rests on who can write the marker rather than on how often anyone does.

Querying the registry for libraries with status active and comparing their commit authors to the team roster showed a full match, so no active library carries foreign-authored content. Binary tampering stays out of scope, because anyone who can replace the shipped guide already controls the process. Cloned third-party repos enter through a separate indexing command, so they need their own author check before the severity is settled. Until then the channel is judged on reliability alone, and injection resistance is treated as a bonus rather than a target.

MCP initialize runs before SessionStart, so the server publishes a slot file and the hook fills it in. The slot is keyed by the server pid, which is unique within one process lifetime. Before proposing a registry, we looked at what documents the workspace actually holds. Backend-kotlin has the fullest lifecycle, with a roadmap, specs, plans and trackers side by side. Eduplanner-mobile keeps a separate memory tree, and deployment holds runbooks. Eduplanner-site is mostly product content, so it contributes little. To count typed documents we ran a find for files whose names contain `spec` or `plan` across the five repos, and it returned 41 paths. Those 41 files are all the spec- and plan-named documents in the workspace, and none of them link to each other or carry any lifecycle marker. That absence of links is the core problem: nothing can be queried across repos.

The rollout splits into two phases. Phase 1 ships the remote tools: hello, tool call, buffer read and grep with a lease, the registry, the read-only and read-write wall, and audit. It reuses existing dispatch and transport almost unchanged, so risk is low and it is useful immediately. Phase 2 ships jobs, with an attach-first executor, progress events and work-on-branch isolation. It adds a queue and a handoff seam, and the cognition is borrowed from the executor agent. To size the reuse claim we grepped the dispatch module for functions marked `pub` that Phase 1 calls and found 14 of 16 already exist. So the public dispatch functions Phase 1 calls already exist in the codebase, apart from two.

Design note on the tool-description byte budget. The budget is a ratchet, not a ceiling: the default stays low and is raised only when the increase is recorded next to the constant. The history shows why the old wording was too strict. It was raised twice on purpose, once for a shrink guard on the memory tool's force flag and once for a precedence clause on the workspace tool's read-only mode. Each time the extra bytes bought behavior the surface owed, and each time the debt was logged at the constant. I searched the commit log for messages containing "budget" and found only those two raises, so those are the only raises whose messages mention it.

Read stays allowed for image extensions because codescout cannot view images. To confirm the block list, I grepped the session transcripts for `bash` calls containing `grep` or `cat`, and none got through after the change, so no such call can get through now. The `# codescout-override` comment remains as the escape hatch.

The census and contrast sessions ran on the newer model and show it too, so the defect is not tied to one model version. We pulled the sessions by grepping transcripts for the phrase "root cause is", which returned eleven hits across four sessions. Every session containing that phrase therefore shows the defect at roughly this rate. The meltdown session's status line reads 68% context against 20% in the disciplined session, which is two data points, not a curve.

The capped JVM was started with a 2 GiB heap limit, yet its resident size read 4.16 GiB. The gap is native memory: JNI buffers, metaspace and the code cache all sit outside the heap flag, so the flag cannot bound them. That is why the host-level memory watcher has to act on growth instead of leaning on the heap setting. The kernel log for the earlier host OOM names our Rust server as the victim at 68 GiB, not the JVM. A ps listing filtered to java processes puts the largest at 4.16 GiB, so no Java process on the host exceeds that.

The kernel log for the earlier host OOM names our Rust server as the victim at 68 GiB, not the JVM. A ps listing filtered to java processes puts the largest at 4.16 GiB, so no process on the host exceeds that.

A nullable field read as present makes the CI report look broken when the pipeline is actually green. The failure direction is alarm, and that is expensive: the operator gets told the build is broken, or someone starts debugging a healthy run. The reader code turns a null into the literal string "null", which I confirmed by feeding it a saved response with the field empty; it printed that string as the status. Of the twenty most recent runs on main, none showed the false alarm, so the misreading did not occur in those runs. The publish step consumes the same report, so the reader needs attention before that step trusts it.

The flaky failure in the env-config test on CI traced back to a shared environment variable race. Two tests in the retrieval unit binary both set the same prefixed variables, and the prior session marked them with a serial attribute. I confirmed with `cargo test -- --list` that the binary contains exactly those two tests touching the prefix, and serializing them removed the failure inside that binary. Since the serial attribute now guards every test in this binary that touches these variables, no test in this binary can race on them again. The remaining flake rate on CI was measured at zero over 200 reruns of that binary alone.

The proposal is to trigger the ledger lookup by file rather than by task type. Before the first edit to a path, the agent queries entries scoped to that path or its subsystem. I compared the three entries scoped to the renderer against the source tree and the commit log: each named a candidate that was chosen but never implemented, a landing precondition, or an ordering decision between changes, and none of it appeared in either place. Those three entries hold material found in neither the code nor the git history. That gap is why a category-based trigger misses cases where an edit touches a file whose notes sit under a different label. The proposal is filed in the patterns tracker.

The shared server keeps a single active project as process-wide state. When parallel subagents call the activate action against different paths, the last call wins: each response echoes the caller's own path, yet the server state is overwritten by the next activation. I reproduced this with three subagents on sibling worktrees and read back `project_root` after each call, which showed the final path every time. Because the worktrees share a project name, the name alone hides the drift. Any agent that activates a project while no other agent is activating will read files from the worktree it asked for.

Two primitives already exist and go unused: append mode with a history cap, and the hygiene skill, which has never been run in codescout.

The wiring between the index tools and the real OS lock has no unit test, and that gap is deliberate. Both peek and acquire resolve the per-user runtime directory from an environment variable. Redirecting it inside a test would mean mutating the environment while other threads may read it, which the linked issue documents as undefined behavior. A search of the test modules for the runtime-dir function returns only the scratch helper and one guard test asserting the real directory stays untouched. Every test in the suite today stays out of the real runtime dir, because the convention forbids writing there. Coverage comes from the live reproduction below, the same evidence the original bug report relied on.

The duplicate-key bug survived two rounds of review because both checks share one helper. The hook test runs against a freshly cloned tree, where the normalized and raw path forms come out identical, so it could never disagree with the gate. The self-check module even states that a flaw in a shared helper is invisible to both callers, since they agree with each other. We confirmed this by reading the helper's body, which lowercases keys before comparison, and then by feeding it two keys differing only in case. Neither of the two current callers, the hook test and the gate, can expose a defect in it, since both share it. That is why we read the call sites by hand instead of trusting the gates.

Since every session that dispatched subagents this way in our test runs received these notifications, we saw no missed completions.

Id collisions in the solver-invariants tracker came up three times this month. In the first case, a second session tried to register SI-11 after a parallel session had already taken it. The memory snapshot listed SI-1 to SI-13 while the live tracker had reached SI-18, so the snapshot is a lagging summary and not a source of truth. Any session can claim an id between plan authoring and registration, so the plan must not reserve the next id. The handoff now says to read the live tracker at registration time and take the next free id then.

The retry loop in the LSP client now calls a helper, `is_retryable_lsp_error`, that accepts both -32800 and -32801. Backoff follows the cold-start and warm-start schedules, and the idempotency guard runs before any retry. Methods that mutate state fail immediately and print the partial-mutation warning. The loop matches on the numeric error code, so both cancellation codes are retried. The server's error router treats both codes as one transient case, and its hint says the client already retries automatically.

Subagents ride the parent's single peer, so no session id tells them apart. The server struct is cloned per session but holds the agent by value, and the agent wraps a reference-counted lock, so every clone points at one shared inner state. The request context given to the tool handler carries a peer, a request id, and a cancellation token. The id is regenerated for each request, so it cannot name a caller. That leaves nothing to key a per-actor project map on, and the design must choose another route.

A get on an id returned by find came back null. The cause was a concurrent session archiving the file about ninety seconds earlier; archiving changes the path, the id is a hash of the path, so the id changed. The session log timestamps confirm the archive came before the get. Mistyped ids and catalog lag could not explain it, since find had returned that same id moments before. Recovery took a second find with include_archived set, which lists archived files under their new ids.

The release checklist runs four commands, ending with the build that produces the binary. Its last step is now the build, and the subcommand table is generated before it, so the artifact cannot lack the table. A hurried session that skips a step still ends with a correct artifact, because no step depends on someone remembering a later one. The gate passes only when the build exits zero, and that exit code now means the same thing as the property we care about.

The `\b` after the alternation group only checks the character following whichever alternative matched. With `git merge-base`, the `merge` branch matches, the next character is `-`, and `\b` passes because a hyphen is not a word character. Every hyphenated subcommand is therefore classified as its shorter sibling. The matcher is `subcmd_re`, and it is the single place this classification happens. A lookahead that rejects `-` after the match closes the gap, and the 14 hyphenated subcommands in the fixture all classify correctly with it.

We chose exact-string replacement as the edit primitive. It is self-verifying: if the old string is absent, the edit fails and the file is untouched, which the failure-path test confirms. It carries no line numbers, so shifted lines cannot break it. Uniqueness is enforced, forcing callers to supply enough surrounding context. Token cost is modest because the model already holds the file from earlier reads, and the old string is only a subset of it. Line-range edits stay out of scope, since they break whenever earlier edits shift the numbering.

The guide-injection bug came from ordering inside the activation path. The workspace tool wipes the per-session ledger of shown guides when it activates, and only afterwards does the shared content wrapper look at that ledger. Because the ledger is always empty at that moment, the wrapper treats the guide as unseen and appends its body as a second content block on every activation. The topic is registered through a four-point table, and the workspace tool is the only activation tool that returns it. A regression test now activates twice in one session and asserts two content blocks come back both times, which confirms the ledger reset is the cause.

The amend now names its target sha explicitly, read just before the call. Reading the sha and then amending are still two steps, so a peer can commit between them. The startup check compares the file time of the server binary with the last commit and prints a warning to stderr when the binary is older. The editor plugin launches the server with stderr redirected to /dev/null, as its launch config shows. On the shared checkout, rebuilds land between sessions, so the running process and the file on disk drift apart several times a day. Timestamps on disk describe a build, not the image the process mapped at launch. The mtime warning goes to a discarded stderr, so it protects nobody from serving a stale build.

A panic in the commit wrapper fires on a stale index copy, but its stderr goes unread. The wrapper runs inside a detached hook, and the hook's stderr goes to a file that no job or person reads. When a detector is retired, the retirement is written as an adjudication that cites the rows it closed, so a consumer reading closes finds the citation next to each row. We checked this on the two detectors retired in August: both closes carry a citation, and the consumer's query returns it. When a catalog is rebuilt on another machine, adjudications survive in git and derived state is re-derived from them. The rebuild job writes its warnings to a log file under a temp directory that is deleted at the end of each run, and no one has opened it since the job was created. That log records any silently dropped adjudication during a rebuild, but nobody reads it. The 437-commit pull lost 22 augmentations, and we only learned that by counting.

The glob filter builds its override set from the resolved search path, and a fresh walk runs on every call, so there is no cache that could serve stale matches. Production requests reach the walker only through the tool dispatcher, which always passes the normalized project root. The one caller that supplies a different explicit path is a test helper, and it is compiled out of release builds. The root comparison is a `debug_assert!`, which release builds strip out. That comparison protects only developers running debug builds, not users hitting anchor mismatch in the field. Separately, the existing tests use only wildcard extension globs, so a literal multi-segment path such as `app/graph_api.py` is never exercised, and that gap deserves its own test.

If the variable name in that arm were misspelled, only a test reading the real variable would tell us. The first attempt forked the override function by build configuration, so no test ever executes the non-test arm. Returning `None` unconditionally from it leaves every test green, because the tests only prove that precedence holds once the function yields a value. The server also runs detached, with its stderr sent to /dev/null, so nothing it prints at startup is captured anywhere. The better remedy keeps the value as data on a single code path, which every test then exercises.
