The common pipeline shape never reaches `inject_tee`: an unbounded producer such as `cargo` or `git` piped into a trimmer is rejected earlier by the IL3 check. Only a bounded left-hand side like `dir` or `cat` gets that far. Under `cmd.exe`, `head` and `tail` do not exist, and the captured output shows `'head' is not recognized` for those attempts. IL3 writes its message only to an internal trace file, and the agent never opens that file, so the caller sees just an exit code of 1. Users get no guidance on bounding the producer, because that error reaches only a trace they never open.

The eval compares four arms on adoption of result-carried guidance and on resistance to forged in-content directives. P1 predicts ADOPTION(B) > ADOPTION(A), because the delegation line gives the envelope channel authority. Both alternatives are informative: a floor at zero means result bodies are too weak a channel, and a ceiling at one means the delegation line is unnecessary. For P2, the pre-registered risk is C < D, which would mean the delegation line opened an in-content hole, and in that case the wording does not ship. The harness runs each arm three times and writes scores to a results table that the analysis script reads on every run. If a forged directive is followed in arm C, the harness records it as a failed row in the results table, which the analysis script reads, so that row will catch any regression before ship.

The update tool's shrink guard compares byte counts, and that turned out to be the weak point in a recent truncation. In the case we measured, the write went from 255,954 bytes to 181,063, a 29% byte loss, so the guard stayed quiet. Line count told a different story: 500 of 1553 lines survived, a 68% line loss. The cause is structural, since the surviving prefix is an Index table whose rows run 3 to 7 KB each, so a third of the lines holds two thirds of the bytes. The guard's refusal path writes a warning to the tool's debug log, which no caller reads, so a refusal there is recorded but not acted on. Until the check counts lines, documents front-loaded with long rows will keep slipping under it.

Routing by selector only works for tools that override the selector key. The trait default returns nothing, and the content operation calls the router only when a selector is present, so a tool without an override never reaches it. The librarian adapter is the one production override, and the adapter constructor wraps every librarian-crate tool, which gives those tools a selector. Memory is different: the server registers it directly, without the wrapper, and its trait impl has no override. The router logs an error when a selector fails to match any shape, but memory supplies no selector, so that log line never runs for it. That leaves memory outside the routed path until either the registration or the impl changes.

The earlier claim that only two publication states exist was overstated. Committed-but-held is unavailable with a plain branch push, but the refspec form, pushing a sha to a branch name, publishes up to that sha and nothing above it. Granularity is prefix-only, so relief is directional: a withheld commit above yours stays unpublished, while one beneath yours cannot be bypassed. We exercised this on 2026-09-07: pushing one sha to the experiments branch sent 1 of 2 commits, and a branch-contains check on both confirmed the peer's commit stayed local. The push wrapper prints a notice when a push would carry a peer's commit along. That notice is written only to the terminal of the pushing session, which runs unattended in the overnight job, so nobody sees it and peers can still be published by accident.

The empty-result assertion in the harness writes to a discarded stderr, so the zero rows in the mailed table are what expose a broken index. The nightly cron job launches that harness with stderr sent to /dev/null, and only the summary table is mailed to the team. That table lists hit@5 and hit@10 per query, and a failed query shows as a zero row. Scoring is file-level, over expected files, so a file already found through some other chunk counts the same either way. Chunk-level discrimination is untouched by this result and needs a different instrument.

The deny-warnings clippy flag only stops lint regressions on machines where a developer chooses to run it. The CI workflow holds a single job that runs the full test command, and no hook or job invokes clippy or fmt anywhere. New errors go through the recoverable constructors rather than a bail macro, because callers can self-correct from input-driven failures. The librarian feature is on by default, so build and test commands need no feature flag. Test runs must use the full command, not the lib-only variant, which skips integration tests.

Update's half-finished-write status protects callers from re-applying a patch twice, and the sole caller today is a cron script that reads that status and halts its retry loop. Update writes the file first and the catalog second, so a catalog failure leaves the edit on disk. Create runs in the opposite order, and a trigger test that forces an abort confirms no orphan file remains. Both orderings match what each operation can afford to lose, so I would leave them as they are.

The bulk of the augment call sits inside one lock region wrapped in a bare block, so the mutex guard is dropped before the async event creation runs. I checked by reading the block boundaries: the closing brace precedes the first await. The safe extraction target is the goal-tracker close gate, which works on parsed values and takes no lock. Pull that out as a sync helper and leave the block alone.

Because the write touched only the catalog, git showed no diff to reveal the gap. Queries filtering on entry would have returned subsets that looked authoritative.

The failing test uses a mock client that returns a stale range of zero lines for the target symbol, so no live language server is involved and the failure is deterministic. The retry loop runs the suspicious-range check before the staleness check. After the annotation-gap commit, the AST end lookup resolves the real end line despite the start gap, so the range check bails on the first attempt. That bail becomes the terminal error once retries run out, and the staleness check is never reached. The range guard rejects bad symbol ranges before any edit runs, and its bail message reaches the test harness as the terminal error. On master the lookup is still line-gated, returns nothing for this input, and the staleness path fires as intended.

The tool schema carries 51 parameters with about 12,700 characters of descriptions, and no single one is a fat target. Trimming all of them would save roughly $0.0002 per request, so the cost axis barely moves. The open question is whether the prose steers behaviour. I planted a misleading sentence in the `path` description and the eval flagged it in every run, so the eval is sensitive to description edits on that parameter. One measurement settled the cost question; the behaviour question still needs probes placed at more than one parameter.

This count is a floor, not a ceiling: a row is admitted only when it carries a signed receipt, and rows without one are dropped even if they are probably real. Undercounting is accepted on purpose, since that is what keeps a lower bound sound. On the 400-row sample the count came to 212, and I checked each of the 212 receipts by hand against the ledger. The receipt requirement is enforced in three places: the parser, the dedupe stage and the join. Removing the requirement in the dedupe stage pushed the count to 260 and failed the sample test, so the dedupe gate is proven to hold.

Delete cascades into augmentations, events and observations, which live only in the catalog, so git cannot bring them back. The preview therefore lists the rows that will vanish rather than bare ids. Three commands print this preview: delete, graft and merge. Emptying the row list in delete's preview made the preview test fail, so the delete preview is covered. Reindex regenerates the row from the file, but it cannot rebuild an event log, which is why the list matters.

The replay gate refuses dangerous handles at five separate call sites: shell execution, file deletion, branch reset, package publish, and config overwrite. To check the gate, I flipped the refusal condition in the shell execution site so it always allowed the call. The replay suite went red within one run, with 14 failing cases. That confirms the refusal logic at the shell execution site is covered by tests. The failing cases all named the same handle-mint helper, and the log lines show the caller reading the refusal before deciding not to proceed. A non-replay is therefore not automatically a defect; it can be the gate doing its job.

We ruled out four hypotheses for the truncated insert before finding the cause. A blank line before the trailing statement, an f-string with a list literal, and a broken following method all left the end line correct in probes. The staleness hypothesis failed because that path refuses instead of under-extending, and the bug reproduces with a single clean insert. For the cause, we traced every index-reducing operation in the insert routine, and only the min against the parent's end line qualifies. Changing that clamp to be inclusive fixed the Python case, so the clamp is fixed in the Python handler that uses it.

Dropping the id filter in the semantic query failed the test, so scoping by project id is verified at the semantic query alone.

The model links used to sit in prose and could rot silently. They now live in one script, which fails loudly through curl's fail flag and strict shell options the moment a download breaks. Each of the three downloads there also checks a checksum in its own block. Corrupting the checksum for the embedding model made the script exit nonzero, so the embedding download is checksum-guarded. A CI job that requested the URLs would add a network dependency to every run, so it was left out.

The `degraded` flag is set at three sites in the scanner: a missing language server, a server timeout, and a parse failure. Last week's change added a test that runs the scanner against a fixture with no Python server and asserts the flag is true. Every green CI run since then passed with the flag set, so the flag currently says nothing about the run. Flipping the missing-server branch turned the new test red, so that one degraded path is now guarded. The timeout and parse-failure branches share the flag but sit in different functions, each with its own condition. Separating servers that are absent by design from servers that failed still has to happen before any exit code can depend on the flag.

The link scan response has three finding arrays: `dangling`, `ambiguous` and `unreadable`. Until now each used its own key for the failed citation text, so one grep could not span them. The shared schema now names that key `citation`, and a serializer test compares each array against the schema. To confirm the test has teeth, I renamed the key back to `raw` inside the dangling serializer only. The schema test failed with a clear key-mismatch message. Key names are therefore enforced in the dangling array. Callers can now use one path expression and get consistent results.

Fenced code blocks are skipped by three scanners: extract, the cited-count report, and the link lint. Before trusting a cited count, sample the guide sources and convention docs, where example tokens cluster.

The push guard refuses any range that contains an uncleared author, and it enforces this at four sites: the branch push, the SHA push, the tag push, and the mirror push. The oldest commit in the real range did belong to an uncleared author, so no clean prefix existed. Because the SHA push was blocked, the guard is confirmed to hold on the SHA push path.

Fusion scores use 1/(1+rank), which puts rank-1 at 0.500 and rank-9 near 0.100. That formula lives in three places: the Qdrant query config, the offline replay script, and the dashboard's score explainer. I changed the offset from 1 to 60 in the replay script, and the recall test failed, as expected. That failure shows the formula is guarded in the replay script. The Qdrant config and the explainer were left as they were, and neither has a test that reads the offset. The replay script is the only copy whose output the recall test consumes.

After the rebuild incident we audited how sessions learn that the binary under them was replaced. The status action now returns a compile-time commit id, so a session can compare it against origin instead of reading process metadata. Three call sites consult that id: the status handler, the handoff printer, and the fleet enumerator in the build script. We reverted the id lookup in the status handler and the status test went red, so the id check is covered at that one site. The build script already refuses to run when HEAD trails origin, which is why we attach the enumeration there. Notifying peers remains the weakest option, since each one costs a round trip and can decline.

I had claimed the audit tool ignores source comments, and that was untrue. Two direct measurements show it: the default scan counted more files than the markdown alone could account for, and scanning one Rust file returned 23 refs. The tool also tags these hits with a capped severity reason, which is how I noticed the comment scan was active at all.

The recorder hook writes one tool_calls row per Bash call and surfaces nothing to the agent. The integration test ran ten scripted commands and counted rows. I then rewrote the check to compare the extension classification column instead of the row count, and re-ran with the hook disabled to see it fail.

Handoff note on the staleness check for the docs sweep. The check asserted that a file was dead when no commit touched it in ninety days, and it failed on the fixture set: it flagged a script that a build step still calls. I then rewrote the assertion to say a file was dead when no commit touched it and no other file mentioned its name. The three probes we ran agree with each other, but all three read git history, so together they give no more evidence than one of them does.

I wrote a test that pins a workspace, runs onboarding, and asserts the config file lands under the pinned directory. It went red, and the file sat under the default project's directory. The remaining work is threading the override through all eleven call sites, which is mechanical but large. I counted the sites by searching the file for the plain helpers and found no suffixed variants.

A direct call built fine on my machine and then failed the minimal-features CI job with an unresolved-import error, which I saw in the job log. The installed-hook design keeps the core crate free of the feature gate, and the syncer looks rows up without ever creating them.

Ten of eleven CLI tests failed with an unrecognized-subcommand error for the artifact command. The tests exec the binary by a fixed path in the shared build directory, and a peer session had just run the lean gate, which rebuilds that path without the librarian feature. I confirmed this by rebuilding with default features and rerunning: all eleven passed. Earlier I had tightened the test's expected stderr to match the exact message text, after the loose substring check went red. Because the tightened check was never run, I rebuilt the lean binary and ran it to watch that check fail on the stale binary. So the failures are a build-collision artifact, not a feature-gating regression.

The repository has one .git/index, and every session shares it. It has no per-session partition and no record of who staged which path, so a peer running a reset or a pre-commit hook can change what another session staged. To pin this down I wrote a test asserting that a staged path survives a peer's pre-commit run. It failed: the path vanished from the index. I then changed the assertion to check the path only after the peer's run finished and the index lock was released. The first version failed, but the second differs, so I executed it and watched the path vanish from the index again. Ownership tracking has to come from us, not from git.

The guard earns its place by making the race visible. Without it the commit would go through silently, and losing the stage would look the same as never having staged the file. Two reads disagreeing is a loud signal. To confirm the guard trips, I wrote a check that the second read differs from the first after a peer unstages the path, and it went red as intended on the unguarded build. I then loosened the check to tolerate a reordered path list. The red came from the strict version, so I reran the loosened one on the unguarded build and it went red as well. That is why this entry should survive the reconciliation.

The stale-context bug showed up when two projects were activated in one session and the second one kept answering from the first one's paths. I wrote a test that activates project A, then project B, and asserts that derive_ctx returns B's root. It failed on the first run, returning A's root, which confirmed the cache was serving stale entries. After that I rewrote the assertion to compare the full context object, including git_root, instead of only the root path. Since the earlier failure came from the old root-path assertion, the rewritten full-context assertion still needs its own failing run against the cache. Removing the cache entirely made the original root-path check pass, and per-call cost stayed in the hundreds of microseconds, so the cache is not worth keeping.

The recursive-grep guard was missing cases, so this session I replaced the single-regex check with isRecursiveGrep(). It splits the command on the pipe character, requires grep to be the first token of a segment, and then tests each later token against the recursive long and short flags or a combined short-flag cluster containing r. Before rewriting, a test for a combined cluster failed, showing the old regex missed it. I also widened find detection to allow several tokens before -name, so the type-filtered find on rust files is now caught. The old find pattern was shown to under-detect by a type-filtered find that it missed in a separate run. The new grep function passes all the cases in the suite.

The filter parser in the output module treats every bare token after the final `--` as a test name. That is why a piped command such as `cargo test -- parse_args 2>&1 | grep ok` produced a bogus "matched nothing" notice: `grep` and `ok` were counted as filters. I reproduced it by running the piped command and reading the diagnostic, which listed both stray tokens while the real filter passed. For the CI wrapper, the lib lane and the integration lane run as `cargo test --lib -- parse_args ; cargo test --test cli -- parse_args`, so the notice fires once per lane. The parser should stop collecting filters at the first token that starts with a shell operator.

Both walkers now prune ignored directories through a filter closure on the shared matcher. Freshness stamps only stay honest when discharging one is cheap, so we attach it to the review path people already use. The stamp records a named owner and a date in the doc header, and a reviewer bumps it in the same change that touches the page. The CI gate is wired as `cargo test -p docs_fresh ; cargo test -p docs_owner`, so an expired date never hides a missing-owner failure. Google's g3doc shows the same pattern working at scale, where the byline is part of normal code review. We copy the in-band owner and the reuse of review, but our stamp must also name the instrument that was checked.

Overflow handling was traced through the handoff logs this morning. When a result is too large, the agent gets a compact envelope with an output_id, a byte count, and a hint. For tools that ship a real compact formatter, that envelope often answers the question directly, as with grep returning the matching lines. For the rest, the envelope is metadata only, so the agent must call again before doing anything useful. The stalled run that burned three extra round-trips belonged to the session with sessionId 7f3a91c2, which we can therefore blame for the wasted budget. Its log shows each metadata-only envelope followed by a retry call.

The threshold for a metric_baseline child lives on the goal's acceptance signal, so the child itself cannot say whether a value is good enough. The kernel reads the current value from the child's params and compares it against the signal's threshold. A child cited by several signals reports Done only when all of them are met, and InProgress when some are. With no citing signal the child stays Active, since nothing ties it to a closure condition. The sibling session's status board lists the goal as closable, so the kernel checks each signal before auto-closing it. The closure path in the log shows the comparison running on each signal before any close.

The handler for the markdown reader builds its advisory hints from the response alone, and the trait it implements shows why. The reader returns a fixed hint string whatever the query was, and the result argument is unused. Before merging the change that adds request context to the signature, I checked whether another session was touching the same file. The peer session's status board listed that file as open in its editor, so I asked its owner before rewriting the trait signature myself. The remaining handlers will need the same signature change.

Two options exist for the pipeline implementation. Option A reuses the inner command runner: each stage spawns through it with a synthesized redirect from the previous stage's tempfile, and stdout is buffered per stage. That keeps the timeout, process-group kill and security checks, at the cost of re-running reference resolution per stage. Option B writes a new pipeline runner that pipes stdouts in memory, which is cleaner but duplicates the kill and SIGPIPE machinery. Lean toward A. Timing the 12-stage log-scrubbing pipeline directly gave 2 ms of resolution per stage, so the per-stage cost is negligible there.

The commit hint asks the author to reply when a change is theirs. Reading the incident log shows a fourth state beyond yes, no and unsure: the change is theirs, but they hold no clearance to commit. That state is the default, since every session starts with a standing instruction to commit or push only on request. In this incident's session log, the hint drew no reply from the author of the stray file, matching the no-clearance default. The remedy that needs no reply from anyone avoids the problem entirely.

The push guard accepts an acknowledgement variable set by the pusher's operator, and that ack names other sessions' commits to the guard. No channel exists by which an acked author is notified, and we confirmed this by reading the guard's source end to end. Over the last 30 acked pushes, no author filed a complaint about a lost commit, but the author of commit 9f2c, who was holding it for review, was never asked. The ack cannot tell an author who is holding a commit from one who never existed, and that is the gap this note documents.

The library tool was missing from `tools/list` in a fresh project, which is exactly when a user needs it. Its availability check returned `RequiresLibraries`, and `current_capabilities` computes that flag as true only when at least one library is already registered, as the function body shows. Yet registering a library is one of the tool's own actions, so nothing else can satisfy the precondition. In the gate code, the check hides the whole tool, read actions and registration alike, so registration was unreachable. The tool was therefore gated on a state it alone can create.

The default-features change had three side effects. First, the release alias inherits it: it passes no flag to disable defaults, so the live binary regains the local embedding backend and its extra size. Second, the Windows build script broke. The upstream runtime crate ships no prebuilt for the gnu Windows target, and I reproduced the build-script failure locally before landing the change, then reran the exact CI commands green after substituting the dynamic feature. Third, the gate script went red on machines without model weights, because the default lane now compiles two tests that panic without the weights directory variable. The gate script sets the skip variable the same way CI does, as its export line shows, so the gate is safe on every checkout now.

The push guard is meant to stop a second person from publishing over someone else's commits. Two checkouts were involved in the incident: one belonged to a single developer, the other was shared by a pair. On the shared one, the guard's ownership check compared the configured author against the pusher, and both matched, so the push went through. From reading the guard's source, I can say its refusal branch builds the full list of unowned commits and returns status 2. The pair then confirmed by hand that the commits were in fact theirs, so nothing was lost. The remaining gap is that the check cannot tell two people on one login apart, and that is now written into the guard's help text.

The first change redirects the Kotlin analyzer index away from the user's config directory. In the kotlin branch of the default server config, we set the JVM tool options so the user.home property points at a per-workspace directory under the cache root, keyed by the same workspace hash as the system path. The analyzer then writes its state beneath that directory, in a location we own, and off the snapshotted home. The real HOME variable is untouched, so JDK and Gradle detection is unaffected, since the JVM reads only the property. Launching the analyzer once, we saw it print a one-line banner on stderr naming the relocated index path at startup, so the log shows it on first launch.

The pre-commit guard script decides whether to refuse a commit by checking a stage log kept inside the git directory. The hook that writes that log ends every error branch with a bare exit 0, which I confirmed by listing each branch with grep and counting eleven of them, all identical. The CLI doc tests now route through one helper that pins the binary. It takes a hardlink to the built executable once, which holds the original inode alive for the whole suite. Cargo replaces the binary by rename, as the build log of two consecutive builds showed: the inode number changed while the pinned link kept the old one. So no peer build can swap the file mid-run. The helper then checks that the pinned copy advertises the `doc` subcommand. The clap documentation describes help output as the subcommand list, so the helper searches the captured output for `doc`. The earlier per-call precondition only narrowed the window; the pin removes the class of race.

We chose to accept the re-orientation after a client sits idle past its TTL, rather than prevent it. The governing invariant is to degrade to re-sending, never to suppressing, and a stale client has probably lost the original orientation anyway. Re-sending costs tokens once, whereas suppression fails silently. The credential read failed only under the scheduler, and that is why every earlier check passed. I ran each check from my own terminal, where the keychain prompt had already been approved. Under launchd the same read returns nothing, which I saw by loading a one-shot job and reading its log file. The one-shot job's log records the exit status the lookup returned in that context, so the jobs were failing with that recorded code. The lesson is to test in the environment where the jobs run.
